title: Random in Every Direction: Why Random Angles Are Not Random Directions or Random Rotations

questions.question: A direction is made by choosing a latitude and a longitude each evenly. Where are there too many points?
questions.explanation: Every line of latitude is chosen equally often however short, so the tiny circles near the poles are crowded. Within 10 degrees of the north pole the share was 0.0546 against the true 0.0076.

questions.question: What fact makes choosing the height z evenly between -1 and 1 cover the sphere evenly?
options: The area of a band of a sphere depends only on its height, not on where it is
questions.explanation: The even choice gave 0.0071 within 10 degrees of the pole.

questions.question: Roll, pitch and yaw chosen evenly give a mean rotation angle of 126.0 degrees. The right mean is 126.5. Is the draw fine?
options: No: the share of turns under 30 degrees is 0.0045 against 0.0075, 40 percent too few, and the mean alone hides it
questions.explanation: A check on the average alone would pass the bad draw.

questions.question: What is Shoemake's method?
options: Three numbers in [0, 1) combined into a unit quaternion that is even over rotations
questions.explanation: A pole turned by it fell within 10 degrees of itself 0.0073 of the time.

questions.question: Why does rotation_angle take the size of the scalar part and hold it to at most 1?
options: A quaternion and its negative are the same rotation, and rounding can leave the scalar part a hair over 1, for which the arc cosine is not a number
questions.explanation: A scalar part of 1 + 1e-15 must not give not a number.

questions.question: What does a test of a random sampler need to look at besides the mean?
options: The shape of the distribution, such as the share in a region whose true share is known
questions.explanation: The share of turns under 30 degrees, and of directions near a pole, caught what the mean did not.
